explanations.explanation: Opens and repairs, exactly right. It's the first month of his first year, and Hezekiah is already working on the doors of the house of the LORD. I think a king who fixes the doors wants that house open again. He doesn't even wait for his second month, friend.

Shutting doors is what the fathers did, not Hezekiah. Later in the speech he says they "…shut the doors of the portico…" Hezekiah goes the other direction and opens them. He's the one undoing the shutting.
Verse 3 says he opened and repaired the doors. Taking them down isn't what the text says. Think repair crew with a toolbox, not a moving truck. So the answer is opens and repairs them.

Impurity is the word. Hezekiah tells the Levites to consecrate themselves and the house of the LORD, and to remove from the Holy Place every impurity. Notice he starts with the Levites themselves, friend. The cleaners get ready too.

Lampstand is a good guess, since lamps come up in this speech. But Hezekiah says the lamps were put out, and he never tells anybody to remove them. The thing to remove is every impurity. A lamp is something you want to see lit again.

Offerings do come up in his speech, but as something the fathers didn't do. Hezekiah says they did not "…present burnt offerings in the Holy Place of the God of Israel." (2 Chronicles 29:7) The thing he tells the Levites to remove is every impurity. So the blank is impurity.
It's the other way around, friend. Hezekiah says the fathers shut the doors of the portico and extinguished the lamps. No lamps burning, no incense, no burnt offerings. That's a house gone quiet.

False is right. Hezekiah says the fathers shut the doors of the portico and extinguished the lamps. They also did not burn incense or present burnt offerings in the Holy Place. Doors shut and lamps out, and that's the mess he's walking into.
True. Hezekiah tells the Levites the wrath of the LORD has fallen upon Judah and Jerusalem. He adds, "…as you can see with your own eyes." It's a serious line, friend.

This one is in the speech, friend. Hezekiah says the wrath of the LORD has fallen upon Judah and Jerusalem. He says they can see it with their own eyes. So True is the answer, and it's a serious line.

explanations.answer: Make a covenant with the LORD
explanations.explanation: A covenant with the LORD, yes. Hezekiah says it is in his heart to make one so that His fierce anger will turn away from them. That covenant is with the LORD, the God of Israel. That's a good place for a king's heart to be.

explanations.answer: Send gifts to the king of Assyria
explanations.explanation: Gifts to the king of Assyria don't appear in this speech. What's in Hezekiah's heart is a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel. He says it's so that His fierce anger will turn away from them.

explanations.answer: Lead the army out against Edom
explanations.explanation: Leading an army out against Edom isn't what verse 10 says. Hezekiah says what's in his heart is a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel. He wants it so that His fierce anger will turn away from them. So the answer is the covenant, friend.

explanations.answer: The LORD has chosen them to serve Him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. Hezekiah says the LORD has chosen them to stand before Him, to serve Him, to minister before Him, and to burn incense. Notice he calls them "my sons." It's a fatherly push, and the weight comes from who did the choosing.

explanations.answer: The king will reward them with land
explanations.explanation: No land is offered anywhere in his speech. The king never mentions a reward. His reason is that the LORD has chosen them to stand before Him and serve. That calling is the whole reason.

explanations.answer: The people will judge them harshly
explanations.explanation: The people don't come up in this part of the speech at all. Hezekiah's reason is about who chose the Levites. The LORD has chosen them to stand before Him, to serve Him and to burn incense. That's the reason he gives, friend.

King is the word. The Levites go in "…according to the command of the king by the words of the LORD." Hezekiah gave the order, and the text ties it to the words of the LORD. So they aren't just doing a chore, friend.

A prophet is a fair guess in a story like this. But this verse names someone else as the one who gave the command. It says the king, and it ties his command to the words of the LORD. So the word in the blank is king.
The elders will have to sit this verse out, friend. They don't appear in it. The command came from the king, and it went by the words of the LORD. So the blank holds king.

The Kidron Valley, yes. The priests bring the unclean things out to the courtyard, and then the Levites carry them out to the Kidron Valley. It's a handoff, like a relay. The mess leaves the house of the LORD one pair of hands at a time.
The Jordan River is a famous spot, but it's not in this verse. The text sends the Levites out to the Kidron Valley. That's where the unclean things go. So the river stays out of this story.

explanations.answer: Out to the Valley of Elah
explanations.explanation: The Valley of Elah is where David faced Goliath (1 Samuel 17). Famous place, but not the one in this verse. The Levites carry the unclean things out to the Kidron Valley. Different valley, friend.

Sixteen. They reach the portico on day eight, then spend eight more days on the house itself. Eight plus eight, and they finish on the sixteenth day of the first month. Quick math, but a lot of work behind it.

Twelve is a good guess if you only count part of the work. The text gives eight days to reach the portico and eight more on the house itself. Add them up and you land on the sixteenth day. So twelve falls short by four.

Twenty sounds like the round number a contractor would quote you, friend. But the text counts it out: day eight at the portico, then eight more days on the house itself. They finish on the sixteenth day of the first month. Sixteen is the number.

True. The Levites report that they prepared and consecrated all the articles King Ahaz in his unfaithfulness cast aside. They are now in front of the altar of the LORD. What one king tossed out, the next one brings back.

The report says the opposite. The Levites tell Hezekiah they prepared and consecrated all the articles King Ahaz in his unfaithfulness cast aside. Those articles are now in front of the altar of the LORD. So the answer is True, and the things that were cast aside have been made ready.

Seven of each. Seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs and seven male goats, brought as a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah. That's twenty-eight animals in all. Somebody had to keep count of that line.

Three is short, friend. The text counts seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs and seven male goats. They're a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah. Seven of each is the number.

Twelve would be a bigger herd than the text gives. The count is seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs and seven male goats. That's the sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary and Judah. Seven each is what the verse says.

Blood. The priests slaughter the bulls, take the blood and splatter it on the altar. They do the same with the rams, and the same with the lambs. It's a heavy scene, and the text just tells it plainly.
Oil isn't what the text says here. In this verse the priests take the blood and splatter it on the altar, animal after animal. Bulls, then rams, then lambs. The blank is blood, friend.
Water would be a quieter scene. The text says the priests took the blood and splattered it on the altar. They do it for the bulls, the rams and the lambs. The word that fills the blank is blood.

They lay their hands on the goats. The king and the assembly do this when the goats are brought before them. The text doesn't say why they did it, so I won't guess past that. What it does say is that the hands go on the goats right before the offering.

explanations.answer: Lead them out of the city
explanations.explanation: Nobody leads the goats out of the city in this verse. The goats are brought before the king and the assembly. Then the king and the assembly lay their hands on them. After that the priests slaughter them.
No basin in this verse, friend. The goats are brought before the king and the assembly. They lay their hands on them. Then the priests slaughter them for the sin offering.

For all Israel. The priests offer the goats to make atonement for all Israel, because the king had ordered the burnt offering and the sin offering for all Israel. That's wide. Hezekiah doesn't keep this one for the palace.
The text says it's far bigger than one man. The atonement is for all Israel. The king ordered the burnt offering and the sin offering for all Israel. So the king is not the only one covered.

The priests are doing the work, but they aren't the only ones it's for. The text says the atonement is for all Israel. The king ordered both offerings for all Israel. Nobody gets left out of that, friend.

Trumpets. The Levites stand with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets. Add the cymbals, harps and lyres the Levites have been given (2 Chronicles 29:25), and that's a lot of music in one house. I'd have wanted a front row seat for that sound check.
No shields in this scene, friend. It's a worship service, not a battle. The Levites hold the instruments of David, and the priests hold the trumpets. Trumpets are the answer.

Censers hold incense, and that's a reasonable thing to picture priests with. But this verse puts something else in their hands. The Levites stand with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets. So it's trumpets.

They don't wait. The text says that when the burnt offering began, the song of the LORD and the trumpets began as well. The music starts with the offering, not after it. Then it keeps going until the burnt offering is completed.
False is right. When the burnt offering began, the song of the LORD and the trumpets began as well. The instruments of David played along with them. Nobody sat on their hands waiting for the finish.
They bow down and worship. When the offerings are completed, the king and all those present with him do exactly that. The king is right there with everyone else. That's worship from the whole crowd.

Heading back to the palace isn't what the verse says. When the offerings are completed, the king and all those present with him bow down and worship. Worship is the next thing the text gives us, friend.

explanations.answer: Read the Book of the Law
explanations.explanation: Reading the Book of the Law isn't what this verse says. When the offerings are done, the king and everyone with him bow down and worship. That's the very next thing they do, friend.
True. Hezekiah and his officials order the Levites to sing praises in the words of David and of Asaph the seer. The text says they "…sang praises with gladness…" Then they bowed down and worshiped.
The text says it plainly. After the order from Hezekiah and his officials, the Levites sing praises with gladness. Then they bow down and worship. So True is the answer, and the singing is glad.

Hearts. The verse says "…all whose hearts were willing brought burnt offerings." The assembly also brings sacrifices and thank offerings. So the ones bringing burnt offerings are the willing ones, friend.
Families might be in the crowd, but the verse names something else. It says all whose hearts were willing brought burnt offerings. Willingness is the word. The blank is hearts.
The leaders aren't the focus here. The verse says that all whose hearts were willing brought burnt offerings. It's about who is willing, not who is in charge. So the answer is hearts.

Levite. There aren't enough priests to skin all the burnt offerings, so their Levite brothers help them until the work is finished. The Levites step in and keep it moving. That's a lot of animals and a lot of work.
Benjamites don't appear in this verse. The helpers are the priests' Levite brothers, and they help until the work is finished. The blank is Levite, friend.
Ephraimites aren't brought in here. The ones who help the priests are their Levite brothers. They help until the work is finished, friend.

It's flipped, friend. The text says the Levites had been more diligent in consecrating themselves than the priests had been. That's why the Levites could jump in and help. The priests are the ones who needed the extra hands.

False is right. The text says the Levites had been more diligent in consecrating themselves than the priests had been. That's the reason given for the Levites helping with the skinning. Same family, and the Levites came ready.

Everything was done so quickly. The text says Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced at what God had prepared for the people, because everything had been accomplished so quickly. The cleansing started on the first day of the first month and the whole house was ready in sixteen days. They had plenty to be glad about.

explanations.answer: The enemy armies had gone home
explanations.explanation: Armies don't come up in this verse. The people rejoice at what God had prepared for them. The reason the text gives is that everything had been accomplished so quickly. So the answer is the speed.

explanations.answer: The king had paid for all of it
explanations.explanation: The text gives no price tag. It says they rejoiced at what God had prepared for the people. The reason it states is that everything had been accomplished so quickly. That's the one the verse gives, friend.
